title_original: UK’s CIISA reveals fresh round of member organisations including US streamers, Paramount Skydance and Banijay
excerpt_original: Support for the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority has swelled following recent high-profile rape and misconduct cases.

blocks.text: The UK’s Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA) has revealed the companies that have signed up and agreed to fund the industry-backed organisation, including The Walt Disney Company, Amazon, Banijay, Warner Bros Entertainment, NBCUniversal, Paramount Skydance and Fremantle.
The publication of the register follows an event in Parliament earlier today to discuss the prevention of harmful behaviour in the creative industries.

All the UK public service broadcasters have signed up to CIISA, alongside streaming services Disney+, Amazon Prime Video and Apple TV+; Fremantle, Banijay, BBC Studios, as well as ITV Plc, Sky TV, and a slew of UK TV production outfits; theatre organisations including the Edinburgh International Festival; music licensing company PRS for Music; and further music companies.

Film companies and organisations signed up include those with significant TV arms such as House Productions and Element Pictures, along with the Film Distributors’ Association, Film London, British Film Commission, Bafta and the British Independent Film Awards.

However, notable organisations yet to join the list include Netflix. A spokesperson for Netflix told Screen’s sister publication Broadcast: “We are supportive of CIISA and we are actively exploring working together.”
It is understood that Netflix is actively in conversation about joining and had previously provided funding during CIISA’s development phases.

Netflix had also recently participated in a roundtable to tackle bad behaviour alongside 31 other organisations that span TV, sport, publishing and live events that was led by culture secretary Lisa Nandy. Jen Smith, chief executive of CIISA, was present at the roundtable.
Nandy had previously rebuked companies such as Banijay for not supporting CIISA, saying she “takes a dim view of company executives who do not take this seriously”.

In recent months, support for the watchdog organisation has swelled following the publication of The Guardian and ITV News’ investigation into alleged sexual misconduct by David Walliams as well as the conviction of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault.

Registered organisations will appear on the register and carry a CIISA registration mark to demonstrate their commitment to the CIISA standards. Registrants are also able to access events, tools and resources designed to help embed the CIISA standards for safe and inclusive work environments.
Organisations that sign up operate on a voluntary funding mechanism which is applied on a sliding scale so that no organisation pays more than 0.1% of UK turnover.
Since June this year, workers have been able to make whistleblowing reports to CIISA. So far, it has received more than 90 reports.

Last week, Channel 4’s Priya Dogra told a CMSC committee hearing that production companies making programmes for the broadcaster would have to be members of CIISA moving forward, including its news producer ITN.

Helena Kennedy, chair of CIISA, said the watchdog is “a new approach, designed to provide vital, independent protection for those who are most vulnerable in the creative sector, and to embed consistent standards for the benefit of all”.

Olivia Bailey, chair of the Women and Equalities Select Committee, added, “Women in the creative sector are subject to appalling levels of harassment and abuse, exacerbated by power imbalances and a lack of protections, particularly for those outside of regular employment structures.”

She welcomed the establishment of CIISA and said: “It is vital that CIISA receives the support it needs from across industry and government so that it can drive up standards and prevent perpetrators of poor behaviour from hiding in plain sight.”
